Cite chapters by number when useful (e.g. "Chapter 3 introduces..."). Do not
invent material outside the summaries. The output is the input to Stage 4
which derives structured systems[] from it, so be precise about what the
book actually says, not what guitar pedagogy generically might say.

Output the prose — no preamble, no JSON. Use markdown headings if helpful.

<<<CHAPTER SUMMARIES
## Chapter 1: Fingerings

# Chapter 1 — Fingerings

_Distillation; backed by `chapters/ch01.md`._

Chapter 1 introduces the two-part evaluative framework — musical quality and mechanical efficiency — that governs every fingering decision throughout the method. On the musical side, Roberts prescribes a concrete string-selection rule: favor the fingering that keeps the greatest vibrating string length, allowing notes to sing and sustain rather than cutting them short by moving to a higher string. Mechanical efficiency, in turn, is defined as the disciplined elimination of unnecessary or awkward hand and finger movements. Characteristically, Roberts immediately tempers that efficiency principle with a counterweight: players should not cultivate a fear of radical position jumps or large interval leaps, since these are legitimate and frequently expressive techniques that provide contrast to smooth scalar movement. The chapter closes by establishing the notational conventions — string numbers in circles below the staff, fingering numbers left of the notes, and T for the thumb — that the reader will need to decode every exercise that follows. Roberts signature move here is the paired-principle structure: he never states one criterion without immediately qualifying or balancing it with another, preventing the student from collapsing a nuanced judgment into a single rule.

## Chapter 2: Chord Melody Devices

# Chapter 2 — Chord Melody Devices

_Distillation; backed by `chapters/ch02.md`._

Chapter 2 of Roberts' Chord Melody method lays out the core vocabulary and techniques for combining melody and harmony on the guitar. Roberts begins with two fundamental voicing types — close block voicings, where notes are packed tightly together, and open voicings, where they are spread apart — and shows how a close voicing can be converted to an open one simply by moving one or more tones up or down an octave. The chapter's governing principle is that voice leading is the single most important force linking chords: in four-part harmony one is really dealing with four independent melody lines, which may move in parallel (same direction, same number of steps), in contrary motion (opposite directions), or through counter lines, which Roberts typically places in the second voice from the top and activates most when the main melody is static. Building on these connective tools, the chapter surveys four practical chord-melody devices: block chords (a full chord placed under every melody note, with voicing or inversion changed with each new note so all lines appear to move together), sustained chord background (one chord held through several melody notes, dropping tones only as fingering demands while trusting the listener's harmonic memory to fill the gaps), common tones (a single note sustained across a sequence of chords), and short chord punctuations (brief harmonic accents that, when played with authority and timed well within the bar, can imply a full harmonic flow without constant restriking). A characteristic Roberts move threads through all four devices: the listener's ability to remember harmony is treated as a compositional resource, so sparse or dropped voicings remain acceptable so long as the harmonic outline is clearly established and melodically reinforced by emphasizing chord tones.

## Chapter 3: Chord Melody Studies

# Chapter 3 — Chord Melody Studies

_Distillation; backed by `chapters/ch03.md`._

Chapter 3 of this guitar method introduces chord melody playing as a craft of layered harmonic decisions, beginning with the principle that close voicings serve as deliberate textural contrast against the broader sound of open voicings. A central harmonic insight is that chord symbols matter less than the voice leading that produces them — functional Roman numeral identity can only be determined from the full phrase, not from isolated spellings — and this extends to substitution techniques where diminished chords replace dominant 7b9 sounds to inject chromaticism into otherwise diatonic lines. The master's characteristic technical instruction is to sustain each chord tone as long as physically possible, delaying finger movement until absolutely necessary, because this discipline directly generates the continuity that defines chord melody style. Two-note dyads are flagged as a largely unexplored resource for implied harmony, particularly in improvisation, while chromatic passing chords (including altered passing chords like m7+5 shapes) serve as connective tissue between diatonic progression points. Inner voices evolve developmentally — from passing tones to counter lines to fully melodic patterns — and the chapter closes by enumerating the complete structural vocabulary a chord melody player should command: vertical textures, contrary motion, parallel motion, counter lines, block chords, sustained chord backgrounds, and short punctuations.

## Chapter 4: Project Studies

# Chapter 4 — Project Studies

_Distillation; backed by `chapters/ch04.md`._

Chapter 4 of this guitar method introduces the practical craft of chord melody arranging through project studies, anchoring everything in a core physical constraint: if the melody note sits too low on the staff, there aren't enough remaining strings to voice a satisfying chord beneath it, with the fourth string serving as an absolute floor for low-register playing. To navigate this limitation, the author prescribes jumping octaves — transposing the melody up an octave as often as needed — and insists that with experience this can be done without breaking melodic continuity. A liberating harmonic principle underlies the entire chapter: extensions such as the major seventh, sixth, and ninth only alter color and texture without changing a chord's scale function, so the arranger is free to reach for richer voicings without disrupting the progression's logic. The author goes further by treating chromatic melody notes permissively — any note within finger range can be harmonized against a given chord form, even if the result is momentarily dissonant — and points out that when melody and harmony move with independent force, surprising and interesting extensions emerge naturally from that friction. The prescribed working method is deliberately modest: develop arrangements that are as simple as possible, trusting the ear to find voicings that sound good while still letting the melody sing on top. Repetition of this process is presented as the engine of growth, gradually building an instinct for octave displacement and voicing choice until the player edges toward something the author frames as the ultimate goal: extemporaneous chord melody improvisation in a style entirely one's own.

## Chapter 5: Chord Melody Solo

# Chapter 5 — Chord Melody Solo

_Distillation; backed by `chapters/ch05.md`._

Chapter 5 is the closing solo of the method — a fully notated chord melody performance piece that demonstrates the cumulative application of every device introduced earlier (close and open voicings, parallel and contrary motion, counter lines, block chords, sustained backgrounds, short punctuations, octave jumps, chromatic substitutions). No new teaching prose appears; the chapter functions as a worked example, intended to be studied and absorbed as one would a transcription of a master performance. The pedagogical move is the inverse of the rest of the book: rather than stating rules and giving short examples, Roberts here lets the solo itself embody the integrated mature style toward which the entire method has been pointing.
